claim: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii divides by multiple fission, wherein a 'counting' mechanism couples mother cell-size to cell division number allowing production of uniform-sized daughters.
source: The unicellular green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii divides by multiple fission, wherein a 'counting' mechanism couples mother cell-size to cell division number allowing production of uniform-sized daughters.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of Chlamydomonas.

claim: CDKG1 acts through the retinoblastoma (RB) tumor suppressor pathway as a D-cyclin-dependent RB kinase to regulate mitotic counting.
source: We identified a sizer protein, CDKG1, that acts through the retinoblastoma (RB) tumor suppressor pathway as a D-cyclin-dependent RB kinase to regulate mitotic counting.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including Y2H assays, kinase assays, and genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: Loss of CDKG1 leads to fewer mitotic divisions and large daughters.
source: Loss of CDKG1 leads to fewer mitotic divisions and large daughters, while mis-expression of CDKG1 causes supernumerous mitotic divisions and small daughters.
evidence: This is supported by cell size distribution data and division counting experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mis-expression of CDKG1 causes supernumerous mitotic divisions and small daughters.
source: Loss of CDKG1 leads to fewer mitotic divisions and large daughters, while mis-expression of CDKG1 causes supernumerous mitotic divisions and small daughters.
evidence: This is supported by cell size distribution data from PSAD:CDKG1 and PL23:HA-CDKG1 expressing strains shown in Figure 6.

claim: The concentration of nuclear-localized CDKG1 in pre-mitotic cells is set by mother cell size.
source: The concentration of nuclear-localized CDKG1 in pre-mitotic cells is set by mother cell size, and its progressive dilution and degradation with each round of cell division may provide a link between mother cell-size and mitotic division number.
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting and immunofluorescence data comparing small and large mother cells shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: CDKG1 undergoes progressive dilution and degradation with each round of cell division.
source: The concentration of nuclear-localized CDKG1 in pre-mitotic cells is set by mother cell size, and its progressive dilution and degradation with each round of cell division may provide a link between mother cell-size and mitotic division number.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data showing decreasing nuclear CDKG1 concentration with each division cycle in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Cell-size checkpoints were first described in budding and fission yeasts.
source: Cell-size checkpoints were first described in budding and fission yeasts (Fantes, 1977; Johnston et al., 1977) and subsequently investigated using a variety of approaches (Jorgensen and Tyers, 2004; Turner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: Proteins or other molecules that couple cell size to cell cycle activation (e.g. 'sizer' proteins) have been difficult to identify.
source: Bistable switches that control cell cycle transitions are increasingly well understood (Cross et al., 2011; Kapuy et al., 2009; Pomerening et al., 2003), but proteins or other molecules that couple cell size to cell cycle activation (e.g. 'sizer' proteins) have been more difficult to identify (Schmoller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: No consensus exists for the mechanisms underlying cell size control in budding yeast.
source: No consensus exists for the mechanisms underlying cell size control in budding yeast, though several molecular pathways have been found to impact cell size.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by the discussion of multiple competing models.

claim: Budding yeast cell size control involves a regulatory loop involving accumulation of G1 cyclins and the removal of the inhibitory protein Whi5p from the transcriptional activator SBF that controls S phase entry.
source: These include a regulatory loop involving accumulation of G1 cyclins and the removal of the inhibitory protein Whi5p from the transcriptional activator SBF that controls S phase entry (Costanzo et al., 2004; de Bruin et al., 2004; Di Talia et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2015; Schmoller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Chlamydomonas cells proliferate using a multiple fission cell cycle.
source: Like many chlorophyte algae and diverse unicellular eukaryotes, Chlamydomonas cells proliferate using a multiple fission cell cycle (Bisova and Zachleder, 2014; Cavalier-Smith, 1980; Cross and Umen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Multiple fission is characterized by a prolonged G1 period during which cells can grow more than ten-fold in size.
source: Multiple fission is characterized by a prolonged G1 period during which cells can grow more than ten-fold in size.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of multiple fission cell cycles.

claim: At the end of G1 mother cells undergo a series of rapid alternating S phases and mitoses (S/M) to produce 2n uniform-sized daughters.
source: At the end of G1 mother cells undergo a series of rapid alternating S phases and mitoses (S/M) to produce 2n uniform-sized daughters (Umen, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Larger mother cells divide more times than smaller mother cells.
source: Size control is evident during S/M because larger mother cells divide more times than smaller mother cells (Craigie and Cavalier-Smith, 1982; Donnan and John, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Daughter cells pass commitment when they have attained a minimum size that is about twice their average birth size.
source: Daughter cells pass commitment when they have attained a minimum size that is about twice their average birth size.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Committed cells remain in G1 for an additional five to eight hours where they may continue to grow, and will proceed to divide at least once, even if no further growth takes place.
source: Committed cells remain in G1 for an additional five to eight hours where they may continue to grow, and will proceed to divide at least once, even if no further growth takes place (Cross and Umen, 2015; Donnan and John, 1983; Oldenhof et al., 2007; Spudich, 1980; Umen, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Chlamydomonas retinoblastoma (RB) tumor suppressor pathway regulates both commitment size and cell division number.
source: Previously we found that the Chlamydomonas retinoblastoma (RB) tumor suppressor pathway regulates both commitment size and cell division number (Fang et al., 2006; Umen and Goodenough, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Mutants that are missing the retinoblastoma related (RBR) protein MAT3 pass commitment at an abnormally small size.
source: Mutants that are missing the retinoblastoma related (RBR) protein MAT3 pass commitment at an abnormally small size, remain in G1 for a normal post-commitment length of time, and then divide too many times during S/M to produce small daughters.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: mat3 mutants divide too many times during S/M to produce small daughters.
source: Mutants that are missing the retinoblastoma related (RBR) protein MAT3 pass commitment at an abnormally small size, remain in G1 for a normal post-commitment length of time, and then divide too many times during S/M to produce small daughters.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: mat3 defects can be suppressed by mutations in DP1 or E2F1 that encode subunits of a conserved heterodimeric E2F-DP transcription factor.
source: These defects can be suppressed by mutations in DP1 or E2F1 that encode subunits of a conserved heterodimeric E2F-DP transcription factor that binds directly to MAT3/RBR to form a stable complex (Fang et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Two independent allelic insertions, lrg1-1 and lrg1-2, were mapped and found to disrupt the CDKG1 gene (Cre06.g271100).
source: Two independent allelic insertions, lrg1-1 and lrg1-2, were mapped and found to disrupt the CDKG1 gene (Cre06.g271100) (Figure 1A,B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by mapping data and genomic structure shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CDKG1 was previously annotated as a Chlamydomonas-specific cyclin dependent kinase.
source: CDKG1 was previously annotated as a Chlamydomonas-specific cyclin dependent kinase (Bisova et al., 2005), and for the remainder of this work we refer to the two insertion alleles as cdkg1-1 and cdkg1-2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous annotation study.

claim: cdkg1-2 daughter cells are larger than wild-type daughters due to inadequate numbers of mitotic divisions.
source: In order to distinguish these possibilities we examined daughter cells from dark-shifted cdkg1-2 cultures and found them to be larger than wild-type daughters due to inadequate numbers of mitotic divisions (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by division counting data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: cdkg1-2 cells pass Commitment in a size range slightly larger than wild type (~205–225 µm3 versus ~190–210 µm3).
source: The cdkg1-2 cells grew comparably to wild type and passed Commitment in a size range slightly larger than wild type (~205–225 µm3 versus ~190–210 µm3), though Commitment was attained earlier (2.5 hr vs. 4 hr) because cdkg1-2 daughters are born larger than wild type daughter cells (Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by commitment assay data shown in Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The relatively normal Commitment size for cdkg1-2 distinguishes it from mat3-4, dp1-1 and e2f1-4 that have altered Commitment sizes.
source: The relatively normal Commitment size for cdkg1-2 distinguishes it from mat3-4, dp1-1 and e2f1-4 that have altered Commitment sizes (Fang et al., 2006; Umen and Goodenough, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to published data on other mutants.

claim: After Commitment, cdkg1 strains stayed in G1 phase for ~8 hr indicating a normal delay period before starting S/M.
source: After Commitment, cdkg1 strains stayed in G1 phase for ~8 hr indicating a normal delay period before starting S/M (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle progression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The large-cell phenotype of cdkg1 mutants is due to defective size control during S/M and not caused by slow or impaired cell cycle progression.
source: Together these results show that the large-cell phenotype of cdkg1 mutants is due to defective size control during S/M and not caused by slow or impaired cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of normal cell cycle timing and reduced division number.

claim: The cdkg1-2 mat3-4 double mutants were as small as mat3 single mutants.
source: The double mutants were as small as mat3 single mutants (Figure 1F), a relationship that is opposite to that seen in dp1 mat3 double mutant strains that have large cells (Fang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cell size distribution data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The epistasis relationship indicates that CDKG1 acts genetically upstream of the MAT3/RBR complex to control cell size.
source: This epistasis relationship indicates that CDKG1 acts genetically upstream of the MAT3/RBR complex to control cell size (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The predicted CDKG1 protein has a unique N-terminal domain of ~90 amino acids followed by a kinase domain with conserved catalytic motifs and homology to the CDK family.
source: The predicted CDKG1 protein has a unique N-terminal domain of ~90 amino acids followed by a kinase domain with conserved catalytic motifs and homology to the CDK family (Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Bisova et al., 2005), but the canonical PSTAIRE motif of CDK1 that constitutes part of its cyclin binding interface (Morgan, 1997) is replaced by SDSTIRE in CDKG1.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and alignment shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The canonical PSTAIRE motif of CDK1 is replaced by SDSTIRE in CDKG1.
source: The predicted CDKG1 protein has a unique N-terminal domain of ~90 amino acids followed by a kinase domain with conserved catalytic motifs and homology to the CDK family (Figure 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Bisova et al., 2005), but the canonical PSTAIRE motif of CDK1 that constitutes part of its cyclin binding interface (Morgan, 1997) is replaced by SDSTIRE in CDKG1.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CDKG1 and its distant paralog, CDKG2, belong to a novel subfamily of CDKs that are distinct from the eukaryotic CDK1/CDKA clade.
source: Our results show that CDKG1 and its distant paralog, CDKG2, belong to a novel subfamily of CDKs that are distinct from the eukaryotic CDK1/CDKA clade and more divergent from CDK1/CDKA than the plant-specific CDKB and animal-specific CDK2 subfamilies.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CDKG family is more closely related to core cell cycle CDKs of animals and plants than the CDK4/6 family of RB kinases from animals.
source: On the other hand, the CDKG family is more closely related to core cell cycle CDKs of animals and plants than the CDK4/6 family of RB kinases from animals.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Wild-type CDKG1 could complement cdc28-13 at 37ºC.
source: Wild-type CDKG1 could complement cdc28-13 at 37ºC, but mutations in CDKG1 that were predicted to make it catalytically dead (K125R) or non-activatable (T254A) (Morgan, 1997) did not rescue the temperature-sensitive phenotype (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast complementation assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutations in CDKG1 that were predicted to make it catalytically dead (K125R) or non-activatable (T254A) did not rescue the cdc28-13 temperature-sensitive phenotype.
source: Wild-type CDKG1 could complement cdc28-13 at 37ºC, but mutations in CDKG1 that were predicted to make it catalytically dead (K125R) or non-activatable (T254A) (Morgan, 1997) did not rescue the temperature-sensitive phenotype (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast complementation assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CDKG1 retains essential regulatory features of cell cycle CDKs.
source: These results indicate that CDKG1 retains essential regulatory features of cell cycle CDKs.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of CDKG1 to complement cdc28-13 and the requirement for kinase activity.

claim: All three D-cyclins that could be tested by Y2H interacted with CDKG1.
source: All three D-cyclins that could be tested by Y2H interacted with CDKG1, but CYCD2 and CYCD3 had much stronger signals than CYCD4.
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CYCD2 and CYCD3 had much stronger Y2H signals with CDKG1 than CYCD4.
source: All three D-cyclins that could be tested by Y2H interacted with CDKG1, but CYCD2 and CYCD3 had much stronger signals than CYCD4.
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The putative S-phase and mitotic cyclins CYCA1 or CYCB1 had no detectable interactions with CDKG1 in Y2H assay.
source: The putative S-phase and mitotic cyclins CYCA1 or CYCB1 had no detectable interactions with CDKG1 in this assay, but both were able to interact with CDKA1 and CDKB1 as anticipated from previous studies (De Veylder et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CYCA1 and CYCB1 were able to interact with CDKA1 and CDKB1 in Y2H assay.
source: The putative S-phase and mitotic cyclins CYCA1 or CYCB1 had no detectable interactions with CDKG1 in this assay, but both were able to interact with CDKA1 and CDKB1 as anticipated from previous studies (De Veylder et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 3A and citation to previous work.

claim: The D-type cyclins in Chlamydomonas contain a conserved LxCxE motif in their N-termini.
source: The D-type cyclins in Chlamydomonas contain a conserved LxCxE motif in their N-termini (Bisova et al., 2005) that is known to be important for binding RBR proteins (Lee et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The LxCxE motif is known to be important for binding RBR proteins.
source: The D-type cyclins in Chlamydomonas contain a conserved LxCxE motif in their N-termini (Bisova et al., 2005) that is known to be important for binding RBR proteins (Lee et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: CYCD2, CYCD3 and CDKG1 tested positive for binding to MAT3/RBR by Y2H.
source: All three proteins tested positive for binding to MAT3/RBR by Y2H, though the D-cyclins interacted with MAT3/RBR only weakly (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Table 2.

claim: Substituting AxAxA for LxCxE in CYCD3 disrupted its interaction with MAT3/RBR.
source: Substituting AxAxA for LxCxE in CYCD3 disrupted its interaction with MAT3/RBR, suggesting that this motif is important for binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Specific binding of CYCD2 and CYCD3 to CDKG1 were confirmed using a quantitative immunoprecipitation (IP) assay with in vitro translated (IVT) proteins.
source: Specific binding of CYCD2 and CYCD3 to CDKG1 were confirmed using a quantitative immunoprecipitation (IP) assay with in vitro translated (IVT) proteins (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IVT CDKG1 bound to recombinant GST-MAT3/RBR and did not require its unique N-terminal extension or a D-cyclin partner to do so.
source: We found that IVT CDKG1 bound to recombinant GST-MAT3/RBR and that it did not require its unique N-terminal extension or a D-cyclin partner to do so (Figure 3C, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CYCD3 was able to bind MAT3/RBR directly.
source: CYCD3 was able to bind MAT3/RBR directly (Figure 3C, lanes 5–6).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CYCD2 only bound to MAT3/RBR in the presence of CDKG1 and perhaps did so indirectly.
source: However, CYCD2 only bound to MAT3/RBR in the presence of CDKG1 and perhaps did so indirectly (Figure 3C, lanes 7–9).
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HA-CDKG1 exhibited some GST-MAT3 kinase activity that was consistently stimulated by around 1.7-fold in the presence of CYCD3.
source: By itself HA-CDKG1 exhibited some GST-MAT3 kinase activity that was consistently stimulated by around 1.7-fold in the presence of CYCD3 (Figure 3D, lanes 2 and 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The phosphorylation of GST-MAT3 was dependent on having an active CDKG1 kinase domain.
source: The phosphorylation of GST-MAT3 was not observed in reactions with HA-CDKG1kd and was therefore dependent on having an active CDKG1 kinase domain (Figure 3D, lanes 1,3 versus 2,4).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CYCD3 is the most abundant D-type cyclin mRNA in Chlamydomonas.
source: CYCD3 is the most abundant D-type cyclin mRNA in Chlamydomonas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and is expressed in a pattern similar to that of CDKG1 mRNA, making CYCD3 a likely partner for CDKG1 during S/M.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CYCD3 is expressed in a pattern similar to that of CDKG1 mRNA.
source: CYCD3 is the most abundant D-type cyclin mRNA in Chlamydomonas (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and is expressed in a pattern similar to that of CDKG1 mRNA, making CYCD3 a likely partner for CDKG1 during S/M.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Histone H1 and GST-MAT3, but not GST, were phosphorylated by kinase activity present in the HA-CDKG1 IP pellet.
source: Histone H1 and GST-MAT3, but not GST, were phosphorylated by kinase activity present in the HA-CDKG1 IP pellet (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Barely detectable kinase activity was observed from equivalent amounts of HA-CDKG1kd protein.
source: In contrast, barely detectable kinase activity was observed from equivalent amounts of HA-CDKG1kd protein (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CDKG1 was found associated with MAT3/RBR only in S/M phase cells.
source: CDKG1 was found associated with MAT3/RBR only in S/M phase cells (Figure 3E) where it is most highly expressed (see below) and not in a control extract prepared from untagged cells in S/M phase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Although S/M phase hyperphosphorylation of MAT3/RBR was observed, no detectable change in MAT3/RBR phosphorylation in the cdkg1-2 mutant compared with controls was observed.
source: Although we observed S/M phase hyperphosphorylation of MAT3/RBR, we did not observe a detectable change in MAT3/RBR phosphorylation in the cdkg1-2 mutant compared with controls.
evidence: This is supported by phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CDKG1 is not the predominant kinase for MAT3/RBR.
source: These results indicate that CDKG1 is not the predominant kinase for MAT3/RBR, and that like its animal homologs, MAT3/RBR is likely to be a substrate for multiple CDKs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of detectable change in bulk MAT3/RBR phosphorylation in cdkg1 mutants.

claim: MAT3/RBR is likely to be a substrate for multiple CDKs.
source: These results indicate that CDKG1 is not the predominant kinase for MAT3/RBR, and that like its animal homologs, MAT3/RBR is likely to be a substrate for multiple CDKs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to animal RB proteins and the observation that CDKG1 is not the predominant kinase.

claim: HA-CDKG1 was nearly undetectable during early G1 prior to Commitment.
source: HA-CDKG1 was nearly undetectable during early G1 prior to Commitment (Figure 4A lanes 1–4) and was expressed at very low levels in post-Commitment G1 cells (Figure 4A lanes 5–7).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Peak expression of HA-CDKG1 occurred just before the beginning of S/M.
source: Peak expression of HA-CDKG1 occurred just before the beginning of S/M. Its level then decreased rapidly in post-mitotic cells suggesting rapid turnover upon entry into G0/G1 phase.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CDKG1 mRNA levels during the cell cycle approximately match its protein accumulation pattern.
source: Quantitative reverse transcription and PCR (qRT-PCR) performed on a sample time course similar to that in Figure 4A showed that CDKG1 mRNA levels during the cell cycle approximately match its protein accumulation pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The CDKG1 3' UTR is unusually long (1.7 kb) and uridine-rich (27% U) compared to the average for Chlamydomonas genes (595 bp for 3' UTR, 19% for U content).
source: The CDKG1 3' UTR is unusually long (1.7 kb) and uridine-rich (27% U) compared to the average for Chlamydomonas genes (595 bp for 3' UTR, 19% for U content) (Shen et al., 2008) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) suggesting that its 3'UTR might be involved in controlling mRNA or protein abundance.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and citation to published work.

claim: AR:luc:G1 expression remained low until the end of the light phase when it increased and peaked near the time of cell division.
source: In contrast, AR:luc:G1 expression remained low until the end of the light phase when it increased and peaked near the time of cell division (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AR:luc:G1 and endogenous CDKG1 mRNA showed the same accumulation profiles.
source: AR:luc:G1 and endogenous CDKG1 mRNA showed the same accumulation profiles suggesting that the CDKG1 3' UTR sequence exerts its effects on mRNA accumulation by regulating the stability of mRNAs in a cell cycle dependent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The CDKG1 3' UTR sequence exerts its effects on mRNA accumulation by regulating the stability of mRNAs in a cell cycle dependent manner.
source: AR:luc:G1 and endogenous CDKG1 mRNA showed the same accumulation profiles suggesting that the CDKG1 3' UTR sequence exerts its effects on mRNA accumulation by regulating the stability of mRNAs in a cell cycle dependent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the 3' UTR confers cell cycle-specific expression pattern.

claim: The large mother cells divided three or four times while the small mother cells divided one or two times.
source: Both populations II and III divided at the same time (13–15 hr), but the large mother cells divided three or four times while the small mother cells divided one or two times (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by division counting data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The amount of HA-CDKG1 that accumulated in small mother cells was lower than that in large mother cells.
source: Moreover, the amount of HA-CDKG1 that accumulated in small mother cells (Figure 4G, lanes 3, 4) was lower than that in large mother cells (Figure 4G lanes 5, 6).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The total concentration of CDKG1 is higher in large versus small mother cells.
source: This size-dependent difference was evident even when equal protein was loaded from each sample meaning that the total concentration of CDKG1 is higher in large versus small mother cells (Figure 4G, upper panels, lanes 3, 4 versus 5, 6).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Both cellular concentration and total amounts of CDKG1 per cell scale allometrically (i.e. non-linearly) with mother cell size.
source: Thus both cellular concentration and total amounts of CDKG1 per cell scale allometrically (i.e. non-linearly) with mother cell size.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data showing higher concentration in larger cells.

claim: CDKG1 mRNA abundance also increased relative to an internal control in large versus small mother cells.
source: This allometric scaling relationship was also reflected in CDKG1 mRNA abundance that also increased relative to an internal control in large versus small mother cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The scaling relationship of CDKG1 with cell cycle stage and cell size is different from histone H3 and tubulin.
source: Quantitative Western blotting from the same populations of non-dividing cells, small mother cells and large mother cells revealed that the scaling relationship of CDKG1 with cell cycle stage and cell size is different from histone H3 and tubulin where the former protein had an approximately fixed amount per cell and the latter was produced proportionally to total protein biomass (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nearly all detectable HA-CDKG1 staining was nuclear.
source: Nearly all detectable HA-CDKG1 staining was nuclear, though we did observe diffuse cytoplasmic staining in late G1 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HA-CDKG1 was only detected in late G1 and S/M cells.
source: Consistent with its expression pattern determined by Western blotting, HA-CDKG1 IF signal was only detected in late G1 and S/M cells (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nuclear HA-CDKG1 concentration gradually decreased with each round of cell division.
source: We determined the relative nuclear concentration of HA-CDKG1 in dividing cells and found that it gradually decreased with each round of cell division (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: N/C in mitotic cells remained constant and nuclear volume halved with each round of division.
source: When we measured N/C in mitotic cells we found that it remained constant and that nuclear volume halved with each round of division (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by nuclear volume measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Changes in CDKG1 concentration were due to a small but significant amount of net degradation as cells progressed through each round of division.
source: This finding indicates that total nuclear volume in dividing cells is fixed, and that changes in CDKG1 concentration were due to a small but significant amount of net degradation as cells progressed through each round of division (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nuclear volume is constant but CDKG1 concentration decreases.

claim: All the CDKG1 protein that was synthesized in cells appears to have been made in mother cells just prior to S/M and it was not replaced as cells progressed through division.
source: Importantly, all the CDKG1 protein that was synthesized in cells appears to have been made in mother cells just prior to S/M and it was not replaced as cells progressed through division.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CDKG1 levels only decrease during division and are not detected in daughter cells.

claim: CDKG1 concentration with respect to nuclear DNA dropped by more than two fold with each cell division.
source: While the absolute concentration drop in CDKG1 was relatively shallow with each round of S/M, its concentration with respect to nuclear DNA dropped by more than two fold with each cell division (Figure 5E) and this ratiometric decrease could potentially be used as a threshold signal to control mitotic exit.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The PSAD:CDKG1-expressing lines had a small-cell phenotype.
source: The PSAD:CDKG1-expressing lines had a small-cell phenotype (Figure 6A left panel) that was never seen in control lines transformed with an empty vector or in transformants that expressed a K125R kinase-dead version of CDKG1 (CKDG1kd) (Figure 6A right panel, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell size distribution data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PSAD:CDKG1-expressing cells passed Commitment at close to wild-type size, ~185 µm3, but then underwent super-numerous divisions during S/M to produce small daughters.
source: Consistent with CDKG1 influencing only the S/M phase cell-size control point, PSAD:CDKG1-expressing cells passed Commitment at close to wild-type size, ~185 µm3, but then underwent super-numerous divisions during S/M to produce small daughters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by commitment assay and cell size data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: PL23:HA-CDKG1-expressing cells showed a detectable accumulation of CDKG1 mRNA and HA-CDKG1 protein in both S/M phase cells and in daughter cells where it is never seen in controls.
source: In contrast, PL23:HA-CDKG1-expressing cells showed a detectable accumulation of CDKG1 mRNA and HA-CDKG1 protein in both S/M phase cells and in daughter cells where it is never seen in controls (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Expression of PL23:HA-CDKG1kd caused no cell size phenotype.
source: As we observed for PSAD:CKDG1kd, expression of PL23:HA-CDKG1kd caused no cell size phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cell size distribution data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The small-cell phenotype and expression of the PL23:HA-CDKG1 transgene were both lost upon repeated passage of cultures.
source: Mis-expression of CDKG1 is likely to be detrimental or unstable since the small-cell phenotype and expression of the transgene were both lost upon repeated passage of PL23:HA-CDKG1 cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B), and this property may also account for the overall low frequency of obtaining transformants that mis-express CDKG1.
evidence: This is supported by cell size and Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: CDKG1 is a limiting component of the normal S/M size control mechanism in Chlamydomonas.
source: Taken together our data indicate that CDKG1 is a limiting component of the normal S/M size control mechanism in Chlamydomonas, that its abundance is tightly controlled, and that its overexpression and/or prolonged expression during S/M phase causes extra cell divisions and a small-cell phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of loss-of-function and mis-expression phenotypes.

claim: Loss of CDKG1 does not eliminate size control completely, but instead alters the normal set points that govern the relationship between mother cell size and cell division number.
source: The loss of CDKG1 does not eliminate size control completely, but instead alters the normal set points that govern the relationship between mother cell size and cell division number.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cdkg1 mutants still show some size-dependent division control.

claim: Other mechanisms must exist that trigger exit from S/M in the absence of CDKG1, but do so prematurely.
source: Thus, other mechanisms must exist that trigger exit from S/M in the absence of CDKG1, but do so prematurely.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cdkg1 mutants still exit S/M but with fewer divisions.

claim: CDKG1 abundance was at least partly controlled by its 3' UTR that conferred a cell-cycle-specific expression pattern to a heterologous reporter gene similar to the expression pattern of endogenous CDKG1 mRNA.
source: Interestingly, CDKG1 abundance was at least partly controlled by its 3' UTR that conferred a cell-cycle-specific expression pattern to a heterologous reporter gene similar to the expression pattern of endogenous CDKG1 mRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The unusually long and uridine-rich 3' UTR of CDKG1 plays an essential role in CDKG1 accumulation in mother cells, likely through the control of mRNA stability.
source: We speculate that the unusually long and uridine-rich 3' UTR of CDKG1 plays an essential role in CDKG1 accumulation in mother cells, likely through the control of mRNA stability.
evidence: This is speculated based on the properties of the 3' UTR and its effect on reporter expression.

claim: mRNAs for cyclins and CDKs such as the CCND1 and CDK6 are subject to cell-cycle-stage dependent differential turnover.
source: Control of mRNA stability of cell cycle regulators is an important mechanism operating in early embryonic development at the midblastula transition (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009), but less is known how mRNA stability impacts somatic cell cycles where mRNAs for cyclins and CDKs such as the CCND1 and CDK6 are subject to cell-cycle-stage dependent differential turnover (Deshpande et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The G1 cyclin CLN3 in budding yeast has been proposed to function as a sizer with its abundance being sensed through occupancy of nuclear DNA binding sites.
source: The G1 cyclin CLN3 in budding yeast has been proposed to function in this manner with its abundance being sensed through occupancy of nuclear DNA binding sites (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Cell division counting mechanisms exist in early embryonic cell cycles of some metazoans where a fixed number of rapid division cycles occurs prior to the midblastula transition that is triggered when the cytoplasmic to nuclear DNA ratio (N:C) reaches a specific value.
source: Cell division counting mechanisms exist in early embryonic cell cycles of some metazoans where a fixed number of rapid division cycles occurs prior to the midblastula transition that is triggered when the cytoplasmic to nuclear DNA ratio (N:C) reaches a specific value (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The ratio of CDKG1 to nuclear DNA changes dynamically during S/M.
source: The ratio of CDKG1 to nuclear DNA changes dynamically during S/M as shown in Figure 5E, so a direct N:C sensing mechanism is possible.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Cell-size dependent effects on cell physiology occur in yeast, where transcription can be size controlled.
source: Cell-size dependent effects on cell physiology are difficult to investigate, but do occur in other systems, such as yeast, where transcription can be size controlled (Wu et al., 2010), and in animals, where bulk protein turnover rates appear to be cell-size dependent (Conlon et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: In Volvox carteri large post-mitotic daughters (>8 µm diameter) differentiate into reproductive cells and small post-mitotic daughters (<8 µm diameter) differentiate into sterile somatic cells.
source: Intriguingly, cell size is linked to developmental fate in the multicellular relative of Chlamydomonas, Volvox carteri where large post-mitotic daughters (>8 µm diameter) differentiate into reproductive cells and small post-mitotic daughters (<8 µm diameter) differentiate into sterile somatic cells (Kirk et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The CDKG1-D cyclin-MAT3/RBR pathway is conserved in Volvox.
source: We speculate that this size-dependent differentiation may be driven by a modification of the CDKG1-D cyclin-MAT3/RBR pathway that is conserved in Volvox (Prochnik et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculated based on pathway conservation and the role of size in Volvox development.

claim: In budding yeast a negative cell cycle regulator, Whi5, is diluted to provide a threshold triggering passage through Start that initiates the G1/S transition.
source: Our model of allometric CDKG1 production and dilution can be compared to a recent model for size control in budding yeast where dilution of a negative cell cycle regulator, Whi5, provides a threshold triggering passage through Start that initiates the G1/S transition (Schmoller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: In yeast and mammalian cells, cyclin accumulation is typically rate-limiting for cell cycle progression.
source: In yeast and mammalian cells, cyclin accumulation is typically rate-limiting for cell cycle progression (Morgan, 1997), but here we demonstrate that abundance of the CDK subunit, CDKG1, may control the extent of cell division.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Overexpression of the human RB kinase CDK6 is associated with sporadic cases of lymphoma.
source: Similarly, overexpression of the human RB kinase CDK6 is associated with sporadic cases of lymphoma (Corcoran et al., 1999; Hayette et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Animal RBRs are phosphorylated on over a dozen sites by multiple CDK-cyclin complexes with site specificity, redundancy and function of individual phosphorylation sites still not completely understood.
source: Animal RBRs are phosphorylated on over a dozen sites by multiple CDK-cyclin complexes with site specificity, redundancy and function of individual phosphorylation sites still not completely understood (Rubin, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: MAT3/RBR has 16 predicted CDK phosphorylation sites.
source: MAT3/RBR has 16 predicted CDK phosphorylation sites (Umen and Goodenough, 2001), any one of which might be a substrate for one or more CDKs and phosphatases.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At least three CDKs are likely to be active during S/M—CDKA1, CDKB1 and CDKG1.
source: Indeed, at least three CDKs are likely to be active during S/M—CDKA1, CDKB1 and CDKG1 (Tulin and Cross, 2014), with the first two having mRNAs that are expressed at several fold higher levels than that of CDKG1 (Zones et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The cdkg1 mutation is completely suppressed in cdkg1 mat3 double mutants.
source: While CDKG1 may have substrates other than MAT3/RBR, it appears to act mainly through MAT3/RBR in size control since the cdkg1 mutation is completely suppressed in cdkg1 mat3 double mutants.
evidence: This is supported by epistasis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: cdkg1 mutants show daughter cell size phenotypes, but pass Commitment at close to wild-type size.
source: First, cdkg1 mutants and CDKG1 mis-expressing strains show daughter cell size phenotypes, but pass Commitment at close to wild-type size (Figure 1, Figure 6, Table 1 and Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by commitment assay and cell size data shown in multiple figures.

claim: CDKG1 protein is produced in late G1 and S/M, and does not accumulate significantly at Commitment.
source: Second, CDKG1 protein is produced in late G1 and S/M, and does not accumulate significantly at Commitment (Figure 4A, 4–6 hr).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Yeasts have a single key cell cycle CDK (CDC28/cdc2) while metazoans have additional accessory CDKs such as CDK2, CDK3, CDK4 and CDK6.
source: Yeasts have a single key cell cycle CDK (CDC28/cdc2) while metazoans have additional accessory CDKs such as CDK2, CDK3, CDK4 and CDK6 (Morgan, 1997) that have been proposed to be tied to the evolution of metazoan multicellularity (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Unicellular eukaryotes also evolved complex cell cycle regulatory systems with multiple CDKs, and this complexity was most likely lost in fungi rather than gained in metazoans.
source: Our work with CDKG1 shows that unicellular eukaryotes also evolved complex cell cycle regulatory systems with multiple CDKs, and that this complexity was most likely lost in fungi rather than gained in metazoans.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis and the presence of CDKG1 in Chlamydomonas.

claim: Both CDK4/6 and CDKG1 are non-essential CDKs with variant PSTAIRE signature motifs.
source: Moreover, the parallels between CDK4/6 and CDKG1 are striking: both are non-essential CDKs with variant PSTAIRE signature motifs; both bind specifically to and are activated by D-type cyclins; both phosphorylate RB-related proteins as their key substrates; and both are part of a system that integrates intra- or extra-cellular information (growth factors or cell size) into the cell cycle program (Figure 2A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data throughout the manuscript and comparison to published knowledge about CDK4/6.

claim: Both CDK4/6 and CDKG1 bind specifically to and are activated by D-type cyclins.
source: Moreover, the parallels between CDK4/6 and CDKG1 are striking: both are non-essential CDKs with variant PSTAIRE signature motifs; both bind specifically to and are activated by D-type cyclins; both phosphorylate RB-related proteins as their key substrates; and both are part of a system that integrates intra- or extra-cellular information (growth factors or cell size) into the cell cycle program (Figure 2A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by Y2H and kinase assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both CDK4/6 and CDKG1 phosphorylate RB-related proteins as their key substrates.
source: Moreover, the parallels between CDK4/6 and CDKG1 are striking: both are non-essential CDKs with variant PSTAIRE signature motifs; both bind specifically to and are activated by D-type cyclins; both phosphorylate RB-related proteins as their key substrates; and both are part of a system that integrates intra- or extra-cellular information (growth factors or cell size) into the cell cycle program (Figure 2A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both CDK4/6 and CDKG1 are part of a system that integrates intra- or extra-cellular information (growth factors or cell size) into the cell cycle program.
source: Moreover, the parallels between CDK4/6 and CDKG1 are striking: both are non-essential CDKs with variant PSTAIRE signature motifs; both bind specifically to and are activated by D-type cyclins; both phosphorylate RB-related proteins as their key substrates; and both are part of a system that integrates intra- or extra-cellular information (growth factors or cell size) into the cell cycle program (Figure 2A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by the functional data and comparison to known CDK4/6 function.
